## Warm-up 

The central limit theorem is **fundemental** is statistics and statistical inference. 

Let's talk about it and make sure we can articulate some fundemental properties assocciated with the CLT. 

-- What is it?

-- Why is it so important? 

Again, we will use this applet for [demonstration](https://www.statcrunch.com/applets/type3&samplingdist)

# Don't peek!

## Summary 

The CLT says that, under certain conditions, we can assume the shape of our sampling distribution regardless of the shape of the population distribution.

This is important because our t and z tools rely on the assumption of normality! 

This is also cool because (as seen in the demonstration), the center of the population distribution and the sampling distribution are the same!

## Last Time 

Suppose we want to test whether the mean home value differs between Wake County and Mecklenburg County. We'll compare 100 homes randomly selected homes in Wake County with 100 randomly selected homes in Mecklenburg County. The Wake County sample had a mean home value of \$461,300 with a sample standard deviation of \$120,000, while the Mecklenburg County sample had a mean home value of \$406,800 with a sample standard deviation of \$105,000.

How do we know this is a difference in means scenario?

## Confidence Interval{.smaller} 

Suppose we want to **estimate** whether the mean home value differs between Wake County and Mecklenburg County. We'll compare 100 homes randomly selected homes in Wake County with 100 randomly selected homes in Mecklenburg County. The Wake County sample had a mean home value of \$461,300 with a sample standard deviation of \$120,000, while the Mecklenburg County sample had a mean home value of \$406,800 with a sample standard deviation of \$105,000.

Let's talk about the intuition behind confidence intervals!

## Formula 

$(\bar{x}_1-\bar{x}_2)\pm t^*\sqrt{\frac{s_1^2}{n_1}+\frac{s_2^2}{n_2}}$

$(\hat{p}_1-\hat{p}_2)\pm z^*\sqrt{\frac{\hat{p}_1(1-\hat{p}_1)}{n_1}+\frac{\hat{p}_2(1-\hat{p}_2)}{n_2}}$

## t* 

$t^*$ is the critical value from the t-distribution that determines how many standard errors we move away from our observed difference in order to capture the desired confidence level.

The conservative estimate for our degrees of freedom is $n-1$ of the smaller group!

## t* 

We can find t-star using the following R code... and we know what this value should be close to!

```{webr-r}
qt(.975, 99, lower.tail = TRUE)
```

## Confidence Interval 

Calculate a 95% confidence interval

## Confidence Interval 

$$
\begin{aligned}
(461{,}300-406{,}800)
&\pm 1.984\sqrt{
\frac{120{,}000^2}{100}
+
\frac{105{,}000^2}{100}
}\\
&=54{,}500\pm31{,}566\\
&=\boxed{(22{,}934,\ 86{,}066)}
\end{aligned}
$$

Interpret this in the context of the problem!

## Which Scenario 

A restaurant is considering replacing its current ordering system with a new tablet-based system. To evaluate customer satisfaction, the restaurant surveys customers after their meals. Under the current system, 180 of 300 surveyed customers said they were satisfied with the ordering experience. Under the tablet system, 156 of 240 surveyed customers said they were satisfied with the ordering experience. They want to test if there is a difference in satisfication between the two systems.

What is our scenario?

What's the null and alternative hypothesis?

## Which Scenario 

A restaurant wants to determine whether the average amount of time customers spend waiting for their food differs between two locations. At location A, a random sample of 40 customers had a mean wait time of 18.4 minutes with a standard deviation of 5.2 minutes. At location B, a random sample of 35 customers had a mean wait time of 21.1 minutes with a standard deviation of 6.0 minutes. They want to test if there is evidence that location A is faster than location B. 

-- What is our scenario?

-- What is our null and alternative hypothesis?

## Which Scenario 

A fitness company claims that its customers exercise an average of 150 minutes per week. A random sample of 40 customers reports a mean of 162 minutes per week, with a standard deviation of 28 minutes. Is there evidence that the population mean amount of exercise per week differs from 150 minutes?

-- What is our scenario?

-- What is our null and alternative hypothesis?
